title: Architecture and UML models
subtitle: Draw the system before you build it: boxes for structure, sequences for behaviour.

sections.title: Architectural styles
sections.body: Architecture = the major components and how they communicate. Common styles: layered (UI → business → data), client–server, MVC, pipe-and-filter, microservices, event-driven. Each trades simplicity, scalability and independence.

questions.prompt: In a strict layered style the UI may call…

choices.text: Only the layer directly beneath it.

figures.caption: Figure 4.1.1 — layered architecture
figures.note: Each layer talks only to the one below.

sections.title: MVC request path
sections.body: Model holds data and rules, View renders, Controller handles input and coordinates. Changing the UI does not touch the rules.

figures.caption: Figure 4.2.1 — MVC request
figures.note: The controller never builds HTML itself.

sections.title: Use case diagrams
sections.body: Actors (people or systems) sit outside a system boundary; ovals are use cases; lines show participation; include (mandatory sub-behaviour) and extend (optional) relate use cases.

figures.caption: Figure 5.1.1 — use cases
figures.note: Placing an order always includes paying.
figures.script:
diagram("direction: right
[Customer] as c
(Place order) as po
(Pay) as pay
[Admin] as a
(Manage stock) as ms
c -> po
po -> pay : includes
a -> ms");

sections.title: Class diagrams
sections.body: Boxes with name, attributes, operations; lines show association (with multiplicity), aggregation/composition (whole–part), inheritance (is-a).

questions.prompt: “1 to 0..*” between Customer and Order means…

choices.text: Every customer has exactly one order.
A customer may have zero or many orders; each order has one customer.

figures.caption: Figure 5.2.1 — class diagram
figures.script:
diagram("direction: down
{Customer | name ; email | placeOrder()} as c
{Order | date ; total | addItem()} as o
{Item | sku ; price} as i
c -> o : 1 places 0..*
o -> i : 1 contains 1..*");

sections.title: Sequence diagrams
sections.body: Lifelines run downward; arrows are messages in order; dashed arrows are returns. They show one scenario of one use case.

questions.prompt: A dashed arrow back in a sequence diagram is…

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: That is an X on the lifeline.

figures.caption: Figure 5.3.1 — checkout scenario
figures.note: Replay to watch control pass between objects.

sections.title: Data flow and activity diagrams
sections.body: A DFD shows processes (circles), stores (open rectangles), external entities (squares) and data flows; it has levels — level 0 is the context diagram. An activity diagram shows the control flow of a process with decisions and parallel forks.

worked.why: A DFD process has 3 inputs and 1 output: it must change data, not just pass it on — otherwise it is not a process.

questions.prompt: A data store in a DFD may connect directly to…

figures.caption: Figure 5.4.1 — DFD
figures.script:
diagram("direction: right
[Student] as s
((1 Register)) as r
[|Student records|] as db
((2 Issue ID)) as i
s -> r : form
r -> db : record
db -> i : record
i -> s : ID card");
